Decisions

What do we regret most?

In the short term, what we did. In the long term, what we did not dare to do.

If you think about the last week, you may regret something you said or a purchase. If you think about your whole life, things you did not do are likely to come to mind: a trip, a career, a declaration of love, an unfinished conversation.

Actions and inactions

In 1995, Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec reviewed their studies on regret. They found a very clear pattern. In the short term, people regret their actions more, what they did that went wrong. But in the long term, when asked about their biggest regrets in life, inactions dominate: what they did not do.

Why? Actions that go wrong usually have concrete consequences that we can repair, justify or learn from. Inactions, by contrast, remain open: we can always imagine what would have happened, and in our imagination it usually turns out very well. And over time we forget the fears that held us back, so they seem less reasonable.

Regret is useful

Regret is not just an unpleasant emotion. It helps us learn and change course. The problem is going round in circles without doing anything.

What usually helps

  • Imagine yourself ten years from now when deciding whether to dare something.
  • Separate what can still be done from what can no longer be fixed.
  • Act where you can: a phone call, an apology, picking up a project again.
  • Treat yourself with the kindness you would show a friend in your place.

References

  1. Gilovich, T. y Medvec, V. H. (1995). The experience of regret: what, when, and why. Psychological Review, 102(2), 379–395.
  2. Roese, N. J. y Summerville, A. (2005). What we regret most... and why. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 31(9), 1273–1285.
